solution.p: a) Over the first interval t = 1.5 to t = 3, \Delta D = 105 - 52.5 = 52.5 and \Delta t = 3 - 1.5 = 1.5 .
Similarly, over the second interval t = 0.5 to t = 3, \Delta D = 105 - 17.5 = 87.5 and \Delta t = 3 - 0.5 = 2.5 .
Finally, over the last interval t = 1 to t = 4, \Delta D = 140 - 35 = 105 and \Delta t = 4 - 1 = 3 .
b) Notice that for each of the three intervals in (a) (as well as any other interval), \frac{ \Delta D }{ \Delta t} = 35.
c) There are three correct statements: It represents the car's velocity, it is the average velocity of the car over the first two hours, and it is the slope of the line.

statement.p: The table below gives the average temperature, T, at a depth d, in a borehole in Belleterre, Quebec.
Evaluate \Delta T / \Delta d on the following intervals
a) 125 \leq d \leq 275 \Delta T / \Delta d =
b) 25 \leq d \leq 125 \Delta T / \Delta d =
c) 75 \leq d \leq 200 \Delta T / \Delta d =
d) Which of the statements below correctly explains the significance of your answer to part (c)? Select all that apply (more than one may apply).

li.p: On average, the temperature is changing at a rate of 0.0072 degrees Celsius per minute over the interval 75 \leq d \leq 200 .
Over the interval from 75 meters to 200 meters, the temperature changes on average at a rate of 0.0072 degrees Celsius per meter.
The temperature is changing at a rate of 0.0072 degrees Celsius per minute when the depth is 75 meters.
The temperature changes by a total of 0.0072 degrees Celsius when moving from a depth 75 meters to 200 meters.
0.0072 is the slope of the graph of at d = 75.

solution.p: a) Over the interval d = 125 to d = 275, \Delta T = 6.75 - 5.30 = 1.45 and \Delta d = 275 - 125 = 150 .
Thus \Delta T / \Delta d = 1.45/150 .
b) Over the interval d = 25 to d = 125, \Delta T = 5.30 - 5.50 = -0.2 and \Delta d = 125 - 25 = 100 .
Thus \Delta T / \Delta d = -0.2/100 .
c) Over the interval d = 75 to d = 200, \Delta T = 6.00 - 5.10 = 0.9 and \Delta d = 200 - 75 = 125 .
Thus \Delta T / \Delta d = 0.9/125 .
d) Only the statement Over the interval from 75 meters to 200 meters, the temperature changes on average at a rate of 0.0072 degrees Celsius per meter is correct. All others are incorrect:
The statement, 0.0072 is the slope of the graph of at d = 75, is incorrect since the average rate of change is the slope of the line segment connect the endpoints of the interval.

The statement, The temperature changes by a total of 0.0072 degrees Celsius when moving from a depth 75 meters to 200 meters, is incorrect since the average rate of change is a ratio of the change in temperature divided by the change in depth (not just the total change in temperature.

The statement, On average the temperature is changing at a rate of 0.0072 degrees Celsius per minute over the interval 75 \leq d \leq 200, is incorrect since the units must be degrees Celsius per meter (not minute).

The statement, The temperature is changing at a rate of 0.0072 degrees Celsius per minute when the depth is 75 meters, is incorrect since the average rate of change averages the rates of change at every point in the interval. It is not the rate of the change at just the initial depth.

p.m: \text{both have an equal rate of change}

solution.p: Since the graph of g(x) is a line, its average rate of change is the same over all intervals. Since the graph of g(x) is going up, its average rate of change is always positive. The average rate of change of f(x) is clearly changing depending on the interval. If the slope of the line connecting the two endpoints of the interval on f(x) is going up and is steeper than the slope of g(x), then the average rate of change of f(x) will be greater over that interval. If the line connecting the two endpoints points on f(x) is less steep, horizontal, or going down, then the average rate of change of g(x) will greater over that interval. If the slope of the line connecting to endpoints of the interval on f(x) is the same as the slope of g(x), then the two average rates of change will be equal (such as the case for the interval 2.2 \leq x \leq 6.1. Based on this consideration, you should determine the following answers:

solution.p: (a) As x approaches -2 from either side, the values of f(x) get closer and closer to -4, so the limit appears to be about -4.

(b) As x approaches 0 from either side, the values of f(x) get closer and closer to -8. (Recall that to find a limit, we are interested in what happens to the function near x but not at x.) The limit appears to be about -8.
(c) As x approaches 2 from either side, the values of f(x) get closer and closer to -4 on one side of x = 2 and get closer and closer to 2 on the other side of x = 2. Thus the limit does not exist.
(d) As x approaches 3 from either side, the values of f(x) get closer and closer to 4. (Again, recall that we don't care what happens right at x = 3.) The limit appears to be about 4.

description.p: Graph of a piecewise function consisting of a horizontal line on 0\leq x \leq 3, a nonhorizontal line on 3\leq x \leq 5, and a parabola on 5\leq x \leq 9 with the vertex of the parabola occurring at x=7.

statement.p: Determine f'(a) for a = 1,2,4,7.

solution.p: Remember that the value of the derivative of f at x=a can be interpreted as the slope of the line tangent to the graph of y = f(x) at x=a. From the figure, we see that the graph of y = f(x) is a horizontal line (that is, a line with zero slope) on the interval 0 \le x \le 3. Accordingly, f'(1) = f'(2) = 0. On the interval 3 \le x \le 5, the graph of y = f(x) is a line of slope 0.5; thus, f'(4) = 0.5. Finally, the line tangent to the graph of y = f(x) at x=7 is horizontal, so f'(7) = 0.

statement.p: Give the x-coordinate of a point where:
A. the derivative of the function is negative: x =
B. the value of the function is negative: x =
C. the derivative of the function is smallest (most negative): x =
D. the derivative of the function is zero: x =
E. the derivative of the function is approximately the same as the derivative at x = 0.75 (be sure that you give a point that is distinct from x = 0.75!): x =

static.solution:
A. Recall that the derivative is negative when the function is decreasing. So we're looking for a point on the graph where the function is decreasing; one such point is x = 1.
B. The function is negative when the function is below the x-axis. One such point is x = 1.5.
C. The derivative of the function is smallest (most negative) when the function is decreasing the fastest. This occurs at x \approx 3.25.
D. The derivative of the function is zero when the function has a horizontal tangent. One such point is x \approx 1.45.
E. Finally, we're looking for a point where the derivative is the same as the derivative at x = 0.75. This means that we want the slope of a tangent to the curve to be approximately the same as it is at x = 0.75. Such a point is x = 3.25.

solution.p: A. We could use the interval to the left or right of x = 2 to estimate the derivative, or we could average the two. We do the last of these here. For the interval to the left, we have f'(2) \approx \frac{f(2) - f(0)}{2-0} = \frac{-19 + 17}{2} = -1. For that to the right, f'(2) \approx \frac{f(4) - f(2)}{4-2} = \frac{-22 + 19}{2} = \frac{-3}2. Our estimate is therefore f'(2) \approx \frac12\left(-1 + \frac{-3}2\right) = -1.25.

B,C. We know that f'(x) is positive when f(x) is increasing and negative when f(x) is decreasing, so it appears that f'(x) is positive on the interval \left(8,12\right) and is negative on the interval \left(0,8\right).

solution.p: SOLUTION
We can interpret f'(x) as the slope of the curve y = f(x) at the point (x, f(x)). Therefore f'(x) is negative when y = f(x) has negative slope and positive when y = f(x) has positive slope.
Similarly, f''(x) is negative when y= f'(x) has negative slope and positive when y = f'(x) has positive slope.
It follows that C is the graph of the function, B is the graph of the function's first derivative and A is the graph of the function's second derivative.

static.solution: f(95) = 40 and f'(95) = 4 tell us that at x = 95, the value of the function is 40 and the function is increasing at a rate of 4 units for a unit increase in x. Functions of the form f(x) = x^n, where n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, are often called power functions.
(a) Use the limit definition of the derivative to find f'(x) for f(x)=x^2.
(b) Use the limit definition of the derivative to find f'(x) for f(x)=x^3.
(c) Use the limit definition of the derivative to find f'(x) for f(x)=x^4. (Hint: (a + b)^4 = a^4 + 4a^3 b + 6a^2 b^2 + 4ab^3 + b^4. Apply this rule to (x + h)^4 within the limit definition.)
(d) Based on your work in (a), (b), and (c), what do you conjecture is the derivative of f(x) = x^5?
(e) Conjecture a formula for the derivative of f(x) = x^n that holds for any positive integer n. That is, given f(x) = x^n where n is a positive integer, what do you think is the formula for f'(x)?

static.solution: f'(x) when f(x) = x^4. Using the limit definition of the derivative, \begin{align*} f'(x) \amp = \lim_{h\rightarrow 0 } \frac{(x+h)^4-x^4}{h} \\ \amp = \lim_{h\rightarrow 0 } \frac{x^4+4x^3h+6x^2h^2+4xh^3+h^4 -x^4}{h} \\ \amp = \lim_{h\rightarrow 0 } \frac{4x^3h+6x^2h^2+4xh^3+h^4}{h} \\ \amp = \lim_{h\rightarrow 0 } (4x^3+6x^2h+4xh^2+h^3) \\ \amp = 4x^3 \end{align*} Similarly, the derivative of x^3 is 3x^2 and the derivative of x^2 is 2x. Following the pattern, it is reasonable to conjecture that the derivative of x^5 is 5x^4, the derivative of x^{13} is 13x^{12}, and the derivative of x^n is nx^{n-1} for any positive integer n.

Because g(x) is the inverse function of f, we know that g(3) = 2. Then note that f(g(x)) = f(f^{-1}(x)) = x, so f(g(x)) = x. Differentiating both sides of the equation, f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x) = 1, so g'(x) = \frac{1}{f'(g(x))}. Thus g'(3) = \frac{1}{f'(g(3))} = \frac{1}{f'(2)} = \frac1{1.25}.

hint.p: If differentiating the entire equation all at once is too much to keep track of, try differentiating the left and right sides separately.

solution.p: Differentiating the right side is straightfoward, and gives \frac{d}{dx} (5x + 10y) = 5+10 \frac{dy}{dx}
Equating the two sides gives e^{x^5 y} \left({5x^{4}} + x^5 \frac{dy}{dx}\right) = 5+10 \frac{dy}{dx}

We differentiate implicitly both sides of the equation with respect to x. \ln y + \frac xy \, \frac{dy}{dx} + 7 y^{6}\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{5}{x}, so \left( \frac{x}{y} + 7 y^{6} \right) \, \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{5}{x} - \ln y, and thus \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\frac{5}{x} - \ln y}{\frac{x}{y} + 7 y^{6}} = \frac{y\mathopen{}\left(5-x\ln\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\right)}{x\mathopen{}\left(x+7y^{7}\right)}.

An equation of the tangent line to the devil's curve at the given point is .
(Be sure to enter the entire equation of the line, including the "y=".

solution.p: Writing the equation as y^4 - 9 y^2 = x^4 - 4 x^2, and then differentiating implicitly with respect to x, gives (4 y^3 - 18 y) \, \frac{dy}{dx} = 4 x^3 - 8 x. If x = 0 and y = 3, then this last equation becomes 54 \, \frac{dy}{dx} = 0, \qquad \text{and so} \qquad \frac{dy}{dx} = 0, which means that the tangent line is horizontal. Therefore, the tangent line to the devil's curve at the point \left(0,3\right) is defined by the equation y = 3.

statement.p: This problem will lead you through the steps to answer this question:

A spherical balloon is being inflated at a constant rate of 20 cubic inches per second. How fast is the radius of the balloon changing at the instant the balloon's diameter is 12 inches? Is the radius changing more rapidly when d = 12 or when d = 16? Why?

Draw several spheres with different radii, and observe that as volume changes, the radius, diameter, and surface area of the balloon also change. Recall that the volume of a sphere of radius r is V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3. Note that in the setting of this problem, both V and r are changing as time t changes, and thus both V and r may be viewed as implicit functions of t, with respective derivatives \frac{dV}{dt} and \frac{dr}{dt}.
Differentiate both sides of the equation V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 with respect to t (using the chain rule on the right) to find a formula for \frac{dV}{dt} that depends on both r and \frac{dr}{dt}.

At this point in the problem, by differentiating we have "related the rates" of change of V and r. Recall that we are given in the problem that the balloon is being inflated at a constant rate of 20 cubic inches per second. To which derivative does this rate correspond?

From the above discussion, we know the value of \frac{dV}{dt} at every value of t. Next, observe that when the diameter of the balloon is 12, we know the value of the radius. In the equation \displaystyle{\frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2 \frac{dr}{dt}}, substitute these values for the relevant quantities and solve for the remaining unknown quantity, which is \frac{dr}{dt}. How fast is the radius changing at the instant when d = 12?
How fast is the radius changing at the instant when d = 16?
When is the radius changing more rapidly, when d = 12 or when d = 16?

li.title: C
li.p: Neither; the rate of change of the radius is constant

static.solution: t gives \displaystyle{\frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2 \frac{dr}{dt}}. Since dV/dt = 20, we can use the values r=6 and r=8 in this equation to obtain the solutions dr/dt = 0.0442097 and dr/dt = 0.024868, respectively. So the radius changes more rapidly when d=12.

statement.p: If \displaystyle L=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \ \ \frac {dx}{dt}=-2, \ \mbox{and } \frac {dy}{dt}=4, find \displaystyle\frac{dL}{dt} when x=8 and y=3.
\displaystyle\frac{dL}{dt} =

solution.p: We rewrite L=(x^2+y^2)^\frac{1}{2} and then take the derivative of both sides with respect to t. \frac{dL}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x^2+y^2\right)^{\frac{-1}{2}}\left(2x \frac{dx}{dt}+2y\frac{dy}{dt}\right) Then we substitute what we know and solve for what we don't know. \frac{dL}{dt}=\frac{1}{2}\left(8^2+3^2\right)^{\frac{-1}{2}}\left(2\cdot8 \cdot -2+2\cdot3\cdot4\right)=-0.468164588784522.

Oil spilled from a ruptured tanker spreads in a circle whose area increases at a constant rate of 5 {\rm mi}^2{\rm /hr}. How rapidly is radius of the spill increasing when the area is 8 {\rm mi}^2?
The radius is increasing at mi/hr.

solution.p: The area of a circle is A=\pi r^2. So taking the derivative of both sides we get \frac{dA}{dt}=2 \pi r \frac{dr}{dt} We are looking for \frac{dr}{dt}, and we are given that \frac{dA}{dt}=5, so we need to find r. But we know that A= 8, so 8=\pi r^2 and thus r=\sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}}=1.59577 Substituting back in to \frac{dA}{dt}=2 \pi r \frac{dr}{dt} we get 5=2\pi \cdot 1.59577 \frac{dr}{dt} and thus \frac{dr}{dt}= \frac{5}{2\pi \cdot 1.59577 }=0.498678

statement.p: A 12 foot ladder is leaning against a wall.
If the top slips down the wall at a rate of 3 ft/s, how fast will the foot be moving away from the wall when the top is 10 feet above the ground?
The foot will be moving at ft/s.

solution.p: A ladder leaning against a wall forms a triangle, with the ladder being the hypotenuse z, the wall up to the top of the ladder forming one side x, and the floor from the wall to the ladder the third side y. Pythagorean's theorem relates the lengths of these sides, x^2+y^2=z^2 But the hypotenuse is a constant length - the ladder is sliding down the wall, not growing or shrinking, so z=12, and x^2+y^2=12^2. Thus differentiating both sides gives 2x \frac{dx}{dt} + 2y \frac{dy}{dt} = 0 We are told that the top is sliding down the wall, so side y is decreasing at the rate of 3, which means that \frac{dy}{dt}=-3, and we are looking for the rate at which the bottom is moving away from the wall, which is \frac{dx}{dt}. We are also given that y=10, so we still need to find x.
Substituting back into the original equation, x^2+10^2=12^2, so x=\sqrt{12^2-10^2}=6.6332495807108.
Finally, back to the derivative equation, 2\cdot6.6332495807108 \frac{dx}{dt} + 2\cdot (-10) \cdot 3 = 0 so \frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{10 \cdot 3}{6.6332495807108}=4.52267016866645

statement.p: A voltage V across a resistance R generates a current I=V/R. If a constant voltage of 8 volts is put across a resistance that is increasing at a rate of 0.8 ohms per second when the resistance is 7 ohms, at what rate is the current changing?
rate =

static.solution: dR/dt=0.8 when R=5 and V=9 and we want to know dI/dt. Differentiating I=V/R with V constant gives \frac{dI}{dt}=V\left(-\frac{1}{R^2}\frac{dR}{dt}\right), so substituting gives \frac{dI}{dt}=8\left(-\frac{1}{7^2}\cdot 0.8\right) \approx -0.1306 \hbox{ amp/s }. (Note that we know the units are amp/s from the Leibnitz form of the derivative, dI\over dt. It is, of course, equally correct to use the expression on the right-hand side to determine the units, \left(\frac{\hbox{V}}{\hbox{ohm}{}^2}\right)\left(\frac{\hbox{ohm}}{\hbox{s}}\right), or, in homework-friendly form, V/ohm*s.)

Water is leaking out of an inverted conical tank at a rate of 10500.0 \textrm{cm}^3/\textrm{min} at the same time that water is being pumped into the tank at a constant rate. The tank has height 7.0 \ \textrm{m} and the the diameter at the top is 5.5 \ \textrm{m}. If the water level is rising at a rate of 28.0 \ \textrm{cm}/\textrm{min} when the height of the water is 2.5 \ \textrm{m}, find the rate at which water is being pumped into the tank in cubic centimeters per minute.
Answer: \textrm{cm}^3/\textrm{min}

static.hint: R be the unknown rate at which water is being pumped in. Then you know that if V is volume of water, \frac{dV}{dt}=R-10500.0. Use geometry (similar triangles) to find the relationship between the height of the water and the volume of the water at any given time. Recall that the volume of a cone with base radius r and height h is given by \frac{1}{3} \pi r^2 h

solution.p: The volume V of a cone of diameter d and height h is V=\frac{\pi d^2 h }{12}. We might as well do this problem a little more generally than stated. (It actually makes things clearer to use variables throughout and substitute specific values only at the end.) So suppose the diameter of our tank is D and its height is H. Suppose the depth of the water is h and the radius of the surface is r. Then, by similar triangles, \frac{r}{h} = \frac{R}{H}, or r= \frac{Rh}{H}. Substituting in the volume formula gives V= \frac{\pi D^2h^3}{12H^2}. Differentiating gives: V'= \frac{3\pi D^2h^2h'}{12H^2} = \frac{\pi D^2h^2h'}{4H^2} This rate of change in volume would be the rate T at which water is being pumped into the tank if there was no leak. However, if L is the leak rate then T = L+\frac{\pi D^2h^2h'}{4H^2}.
Note that since we have to have consistent units of length, and the answer is in cubic centimeters per minute, the lengths given in meters have to be converted to centimeters.
Thus, substituting L = 10500,\quad D = 550,\quad H = 700, \quad h = 250,\quad h' = 28 we obtain T = 10500 + \frac{\pi*550^2*250^2*28}{4*700^2} \approx 859011 \hbox{cm}^3/\hbox{min}.

critical points (enter as a comma-separated list): x =

solution.p: From the graph, we see that f(x) appears to have one critical point, at x=0, and two inflection points, one between 0 and 1 and the other between 0 and -1.
To find the critical points, we set f'(x) = 0. Since f'(x) = 3(-2(9)x) e^{-9 x^2} = 0, there is one solution, x = 0. The only critical point is at x=0.

To find the inflection points, we find f''(x) and determine where it is zero. f''(x) = 3( -2(9) e^{-9 x^2} + 4(9)^2 x^2 e^{-9 x^2} = 54 e^{-9 x^2} ( -1 + 18 x^2 ). For this to be zero, we must have -1 + 18 x^2 = 0, or x = \pm 1/\sqrt{18}. There are exactly two inflection points, at x = -1/\sqrt{18} \approx -0.236 and x = 1/\sqrt{18} \approx 0.236.

static.solution:
1. It appears that this function has a local maximum at about x = 3, and a local minimum at about x = 6. Note that because we're told that the function is given for the open interval (0,10) the endpoints are not properly critical points, or maxima/minima.
2. If the table gives values of the derivative, critical points occur where f'(x) = 0. Since f' is continuous, such a point occurs between 0 and 1, so there is a critical point somewhere around 0.5. static.solution:
f(x) = a - a e^{-b x}, we find its derivative using the chain rule: f'(x) = ab e^{-b x}. Exponentials are always positive, so that, given that a > 0 and b > 0, we must have f'(x) > 0 and we know that f(x) must be increasing.
Then f''(x) = -a b^2 e^{-b x} \lt 0, so the function must be concave down.

statement.p: Find constants a and b in the function f(x)={a x^{b}\over \ln(x)} such that f(\frac{1}{4})=1 and the function has a local minimum at x=\frac{1}{4}.

static.solution:
f(x) = {ax^b\over \ln(x)}, we have f'(x) = {a b x^{b-1} \ln(x) - a x^{b-1} \over (\ln x)^2} = {a x^{b-1}\over(\ln x)^2} (b\ln(x) - 1). We want f(\frac{1}{4})=1, and since this is to be a minimum, we require f'(\frac{1}{4})=0. These conditions give
f(1/4) = {a\over 4^b \ln(1/4)} = -{a\over 4^b ln(4)} = 1 and f'(1/4) = {a (1/4)^{b-1}\over(\ln(1/4))^2} (b\ln(1/4) - 1) = 0.
Since a (1/4)^{b-1}\over(\ln(1/4))^2 is non-zero, we can divide both sides of the second equation by this term to obtain b \ln(1/4) - 1 = 0. This implies b= 1/\ln(1/4) = -1/\ln(4). Plugging b=-1/\ln(4) into the first equation gives us {a\over 4^{-1/\ln(4)} \ln(1/4)} = 1, or a = 4^{-1/\ln(4)} \ln(1/4) = {-\ln(4)\over 4^{1/\ln(4)}}. How do we know we have a minimum at x=\frac{1}{4} and not a maximum? Since f'(x) = {a x^{b-1}\over(\ln x)^2} (b\ln(x) - 1) and a \lt 0, the first term, a x^{b-1}\over(\ln x)^2, is negative. Then for x \lt \frac{1}{4} the second term is positive, while for x > \frac{1}{4} it is negative, so the derivative is negative to the left of x = \frac{1}{4} and positive to the right, and f(\frac{1}{4}) is a local minimum.

global maximum at t =
global minimum at t =

static.solution:
g'(t) = 7\cdot e^{- t} - 7 te^{- t} = 7 (1 - t)e^{- t}, so the critical point is t=1/1.
Since g'(t)>0 for 0\lt t\lt 1/1 and g'(t)\lt 0 for t>1/1, the critical point is a local maximum.
As t\to\infty, the value of g(t)\to0, and as t\to0^+, the value of g(t)\to0. Thus, the local maximum at t=1/1 is a global maximum of g(1/1)={7\over 1} e^{-1} = {7\over e}. In addition, the value of g(t) is positive for all t>0; it tends to 0 but never reaches 0. Thus, there is no global minimum.

statement.p: For some positive constant C, a patient's temperature change, T, due to a dose, D, of a drug is given by T = \left(\frac{C}{2} - \frac{D}{3}\right)D^2.
What dosage maximizes the temperature change?
The sensitivity of the body to the drug is defined as dT/dD. What dosage maximizes sensitivity?

solution.p: SOLUTION
We have T(D) = \left(\frac{C}{2} - \frac{D}{3}\right)D^2 = \frac{CD^2}{2}-\frac{D^3}{3}, and so \frac{dT}{dD} = CD-D^2 = D(C-D).
Since, by this formula, dT/dD is zero when D=0 or D=C, negative when D>C, and positive when D\lt C, we have (by the first derivative test) that the temperature change is maximized when D=C.

The sensitivity is dT/dD = CD-D^2; its derivative is d^2T/dD^2 = C-2D, which is zero if D= C/2, negative if D> C/2, and positive if D\lt C/2. Thus by the first derivative test the sensitivity is maximized at D=C/2.

solution.p: The volume of the parcel is x^2y, and the constraints say that 4x+y=108, so V(x) = x^2(108-4x). We know x>0, also x\lt y=108-4x so 5x\lt 108, hence x\lt 21.6. Thus the domain of V is (0,21.6). Note that V'(x)=216x-12x^2=12x(18-x), so V'(x)>0 and V is increasing when 0\lt x\lt 18, and V'(x)\lt 0 and V is decreasing when 18\lt x. Thus the maximum volume occurs when x=18 and y=36, giving a maximum of 11664 cubic inches.

statement.p: An open box is to be made out of a 9-inch by 14-inch piece of cardboard by cutting out squares of equal size from the four corners and bending up the sides. If the box needs to be at least 1 inch deep, and no more than 3 inches deep, find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum volumes.

solution.p: You have a rectangle of size 9 by 14, and you cut a square out of each corner. Say each square has length x. Then when you fold the rectangle up, the height of the resulting box is x and the length is 14-2 x while the width is 9 -2 x. So the volume of the box is V=l \cdot w \cdot h = (14 -2 x) (9 -2 x)x= (126-46 x +4 x^2)x=126 x-46 x^2+4x^3 Taking the derivative and setting it equal to 0 gives V'=126-2\cdot 46 x+ 12x^2 =0 Using the quadratic formula, we get that x=\frac{2\cdot46\pm\sqrt{4\cdot46^2-4\cdot 12\cdot 126}}{2\cdot 12}= 1.7853 \mbox{ or } 5.88136762124075 But if x=5.88136762124075, then the width of the box, which is 9-2 x, is negative. So the height is x=1.7853.

Plugging back in, the length of the box is 14-2x=14-2\cdot1.7853=10.4294 and the width is 9-2x=9-2\cdot1.7853=5.4294 And so the volume at the local extremum is 10.4294 \cdot 5.4294 \cdot 1.7853 = 101.093.
We also calculate the volume at the endpoints, x=1 and x=3. (14-2)(9-2)\cdot 1 = 84, \mbox{ and } (14-6)(9-6)\cdot 3 = 72
So the absolute maximum of volume is 101.093 and the absolute minimum of volume is 72.

solution.p: A rectangle has sides x and y. Then the total cost of the fencing is C=6 x + 6 x + 6 y + 14 y= 12 x + 20 y We are trying to minimize this function, but we need to reduce it to one variable. However, we are also given that the area of this rectangle is 290. Thus, xy=290, and solving for one of the variables, y=\frac{290}{x}.

Substituting back into the cost function, we get C= 12 x+ 20 \left(\frac{290}{x} \right) = 12 x+ 5800 x^{-1} Take the derivative and set it equal to 0. statement.p: Your task is to estimate how far an object traveled during the time interval 0 \leq t \leq 8, but you only have the following data about the velocity of the object.

To get an idea of what the velocity function might look like, you pick up a black pen, plot the data points, and connect them by curves. Your sketch looks something like the black curve in the graph below.

You decide to use a left endpoint Riemann sum to estimate the total displacement. So, you pick up a blue pen and draw rectangles whose height is determined by the velocity measurement at the left endpoint of each one-second interval. By using the left endpoint Riemann sum as an approximation, you are assuming that the actual velocity is approximately constant on each one-second interval (or, equivalently, that the actual acceleration is approximately zero on each one-second interval), and that the velocity and acceleration have discontinuous jumps every second. This assumption is probably incorrect because it is likely that the velocity and acceleration change continuously over time. However, you decide to use this approximation anyway since it seems like a reasonable approximation to the actual velocity given the limited amount of data.
(A) Using the left endpoint Riemann sum, find approximately how far the object traveled.
Total displacement = ft
Total distance traveled = ft

Using the same data, you also decide to estimate how far the object traveled using a right endpoint Riemann sum. So, you sketch the curve again with a black pen, and draw rectangles whose height is determined by the velocity measurement at the right endpoint of each one-second interval.
(B) Using the right endpoint Riemann sum, find approximately how far the object traveled.
Total displacement = ft
Total distance traveled = ft

static.solution:
Solution:
Using the left endpoint Riemann sum, the total displacement is the net area of the light blue shaded rectangles, and the total distance is the absolute area of the light blue shaded rectangles.
Total displacement = -1 - 2 - 1 - 2+1+3+1+2 = 1 feet.
Total distance = |-1|+|-2|+|-1|+|-2|+|1|+|3|+|1|+|2| = 13 feet.
We can also make similar calculations using the right endpoint Riemann sum.
Total displacement = -2 - 1 - 2+1+3+1+2+4 = 6 feet.
Total distance = |-2|+|-1|+|-2|+|1|+|3|+|1|+|2|+|4| = 16 feet.

statement.p: The following table gives the the approximate amount of emissions, E, of nitrogen oxides in millions of metric tons per year in the US. Let t be the number of years since 1940 and E=f(t).
Estimate the integral: \int_0^{50}{f(t)dt} \approx

p.em: Be sure that you know what the units of your answer are, and what its meaning is!
(Original data from the Statistical Abstract of the US, 1992)

solution.p: The integral \int_0^{50}{f(t)dt} represents the total emissions of nitrogen oxides, in millions of metric tons, during the period 1940 to 1990.

We estimate the integral using left- and right-hand sums: \mbox{Left sum} = (6.9)(10) + (9.2)(10) + (13.4)(10) + (19)(10) + (20.4)(10) = 689, and \mbox{Right sum} = (9.2)(10) + (13.4)(10) + (19)(10) + (20.4)(10) + (19.9)(10) = 819. We can then average the left- and right-hand sums to find the best estimate of the integral: \int_0^{50}{f(t)dt} \approx {{689 + 819} \over 2} = 754 \mbox{ million metric tons.} Between 1940 and 1990, about 754 million metric tons of nitrogen oxides were emitted.

statement.p: Evaluate the definite integral \int_{ 0 } ^ { \pi } 4 \sin(x) dx

solution.p: This integration can be done because we know that the derivative with respect to x of \cos(x) is -\sin(x). So we obtain a -\sin(x) inside the integral, and we can then integrate to obtain \cos(x). Of course, since there isn't a minus sign inside the integral, we'll have to multiply inside and outside by -1 (which doesn't change the value of course): \begin{aligned} \int_0^\pi 4 \sin(x) dx \amp = -4 \int_0^\pi (-\sin(x)) dx \\ \amp = -4 \left( \cos(x) \bigg|_0^\pi \right) \\ \amp = -4 ( \cos(\pi) - \cos(0) ) = -4 (-1-1) = 2 \cdot 4 = 8 \end{aligned}

Use the Fundamental Theorem to determine the value of b if the area under the graph of f(x) = 7 x between x = 1 and x = b is equal to 168. Assume b>1.

static.solution: f(x) = 7 x between x=1 and x = b is given by \int_1^b (7 x) dx. Using the Fundamental Theorem to evaluate the integral: \hbox{Area } = \frac{7}{2} x^2 \bigg|_1^b = \frac{7}{2} b^2 - \frac{7}{2}. Since the area is 168, we have \frac{7}{2} b^2 - \frac{7}{2} = 168, so \frac{7}{2} b^2 = \frac{343}{2}, and thus b^2 = 49,\quad\hbox{or}\quad b = \pm 7. Since b is larger than 1, we have b = 7.

p.em: (Note that you can do this in two different ways!)

static.solution:
x=4, we are given that f(4)=0. Moving to the left on the interval 2 \lt x \lt 4, we have f'(x) = -1, and we can find f(2) by knowing that the change in f(x) over this interval is equal to the area under f'(x) between x=2 and x=4. Thus f(4) - f(2) = (-1)(2), so that f(2) = f(4) - (2)(-1) = 2. Similarly, continuing back to x=0, f(0) = f(2) - (1)(1) - (1)(-1) = 2
Moving to the right from x=4, we know that f'(x) = 1 on 4 \lt x \lt 5. So, as before, f(5) = f(4) + (1)(1) = 1. Similarly, continuing to x=7, f(7) = f(5) + (1)(-3) + (1)(1) = -1.
Then, the value of the integral \int_0^7 f'(x)\,dx is given by the sum \int_0^7 f'(x)\,dx = (-1)(1) + (1)(1) + (-1)(2) + (1)(1) + (-3)(1) + (1)(1) = -3.
Alternatively, knowing f(7)=-1 and f(0)=2 and using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we have \int_0^7 f'(x)\,dx=f(7)-f(0) = (-1) - (2) = -3.

In Section 2.5, we learned the Chain Rule and how it can be applied to find the derivative of a composite function. In particular, if u is a differentiable function of x, and f is a differentiable function of u(x), then \frac{d}{dx} \left[ f(u(x)) \right] = f'(u(x)) \cdot u'(x). In words, we say that the derivative of a composite function c(x) = f(u(x)), where f is considered the "outer" function and u the "inner" function, is "the derivative of the outer function, evaluated at the inner function, times the derivative of the inner function."

solution.p: a. (i) The derivative of g(x) = e^{3x} is g'(x) = 3e^{3x}\ln\mathopen{}\left(e\right).
(ii) The derivative of h(x) = \sin(5x+1) is h'(x) = 5\cos\mathopen{}\left(5x+1\right).
(iii) The derivative of p(x) = \arctan(2x) is p'(x) = 2\frac{1}{1+\left(2x\right)^{2}}.
(iv) The derivative of q(x) = (2-7x)^4 is q'(x) = -28\mathopen{}\left(2-7x\right)^{3}.
(v) The derivative of r(x) = 3^{4-11x} is r'(x) = -11\ln\mathopen{}\left(3\right)\cdot 3^{4-11x}.
b. (i) The general antiderivative of m(x) = e^{3x} is \frac{1}{3} e^{3x}, because the derivative of \frac{1}{3}e^{3x}+C is e^{3x}.
(ii) The general antiderivative of n(x) = \cos(5x+1) is \frac{1}{5}\sin\mathopen{}\left(5x+1\right)+C, because the derivative of \frac{1}{5}\sin\mathopen{}\left(5x+1\right)+C is n(x) = \cos(5x+1).
(iii) The general antiderivative of \displaystyle s(x) = \frac{1}{1+4x^2} is \frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\mathopen{}\left(2x\right)+C.
(iv) The general antiderivative of v(x) = (2-7x)^3 is \frac{1}{-7\cdot 4} (2-7x)^4+C;
(v) The general antiderivative of w(x) = 3^{4-11x} is \frac{1}{\ln(3)\cdot(-11)} 3^{4-11x}+C;
(c) (i) The general antiderivative of a(x) = \cos(\pi x) is \frac{1}{\pi }\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right)+C;
(ii) The general antiderivative of b(x) = (4x+7)^{11} is \frac{1}{4\cdot 12} (4x+7)^{12} +C;
(iii) The general antiderivative of c(x) = xe^{x^2} is \frac{1}{2}e^{x^{2}}+C;

hint.p: Remember that the derivative of \sec x is \sec x \tan x.
Let u = \sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right). Don't forget the chain rule when you find du.
Remember that to integrate something of the form \displaystyle \frac{1}{u^8} you should rewrite as u^{-8} and then use power rule.

solution.p: Let u=\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right). Then we take the derivative of both sides to get du = -5\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right) \, dx

You can do the next step in different ways, but one way is to solve for dx. Since du = -5\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right) \, dx, we divide over to get that dx=\frac{1}{-5\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)} \, du Then we substitute back into the original integral. \int \frac{8 \sec(-5 x)\tan(-5 x)}{\sec^{8}(-5 x)} \, dx = \int \frac{8 \sec(-5 x)\tan(-5 x)}{u^{8}} \frac{1}{-5\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\tan\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)} \, du Which simplifies to \int -\frac{1.6}{u^{8}}du

Now, this is one of our basic integrals because we can write it as \displaystyle \int -1.6 u^{-8} \, du and thus we can integrate it. Constants in front just stay multiplied so we get \int -1.6 u^{-8} \, du = \frac{-1.6}{-7} u^{-7}+C Finally, make sure you put it back in terms of the original variable, which in this case is 'x'. So we substitute back in for 'u', which was \sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right). Thus the final answer to this integral is \int \frac{8 \sec(-5 x)\tan(-5 x)}{\sec^{8}(-5 x)} \, dx = 0.228571\mathopen{}\left(\sec\mathopen{}\left(-5x\right)\right)^{-7}+C

statement.p: Consider the integral \displaystyle \int\,2\,x^{4}\,(x^{5} + 1)\,dx. In the following, we will evaluate the integral using two methods.
A. First, rewrite the integral by multiplying out the integrand:
Then evaluate the resulting integral term-by-term:
B. Next, rewrite the integral using the substitution w = x^{5} + 1:
Evaluate this integral (and back-substitute for w) to find the value of the original integral:
C. How are your expressions from parts (A) and (B) different? What is the difference between the two? (Ignore the constant of integration.)
(answer from B)-(answer from A) =
Are both of the answers correct? (Be sure you can explain why they are!)

static.solution:
A. \int\,2\,x^{4}\,(x^{5} + 1)\,dx = \int\,2\,x^{9} + 2\,x^{4}\,dx. Thus, antidifferentiating term-by-term, we get \int\,2\,x^{4}\,(x^{5} + 1)\,dx = {1\over5}\,x^{10} + {2\over5}\,x^{5} + C.
B. \int\,2\,x^{4}\,(x^{5} + 1)\,dx = \int\,{2\over5}\,w\,dw. Thus, antidifferentiating, we get \int\,2\,x^{4}\,(x^{5} + 1)\,dx = {1\over5}\,w^2 + C = {1\over5}\,(x^{5} + 1)^2 + C.
C. To see the difference between these two answers, we expand the second: (x^{5} + 1)^2 = x^{10} + 2\,x^{5} + 1, so the difference is ({1\over5} (x^{10} + 2\,x^{5} + 1)) - ({1\over5} \,x^{10} + {2\over5}\,x^{5}) = {1\over5}. That is, the difference is a constant! This is completely reasonable: the antiderivative is only determined up to a constant, and the arbitrary constant C that we get for the most general antiderivative will adjust for this difference.

solution.p: Let u=x and dv=\sec^{2}\mathopen{}\left(-8x\right)dx.
Then du=dx and v=\frac{1}{-8} \tan(-8 x).

The integration by parts formula says that \int u \, dv = u\cdot v - \int v \, du So, substituting in, we get that \int x \sec^{2}\mathopen{}\left(-8x\right) \, dx = x \cdot \frac{1}{-8} \tan(-8 x) - \int \frac{1}{-8} \tan(-8 x) \, dx =\frac{1}{-8} x \tan(-8 x) - \int \frac{1}{-8} \tan(-8 x) \, dx Unfortunately, the integral is not Basic, but we can rewrite it and integrate it using u-substitution. \frac{1}{-8} x \tan(-8 x) - \int \frac{1}{-8} \frac{\sin(-8 x)}{\cos(-8 x)} \, dx Let u=\cos(-8 x) so du = + 8 \sin(-8 x) \, dx and solving for dx gives us dx=\frac{du}{ + 8 \sin(-8 x)}.

Substituting back into the integral gives us: \int \frac{1}{-8} \frac{\sin(-8 x)}{\cos(-8 x)} \, dx = \int \frac{1}{-8} \frac{\sin(-8 x)}{u} \, \frac{du}{ + 8 \sin(-8 x)} = \int \frac{-1}{64} \frac{du}{u} This integrates to \frac{-1}{64} \ln(u) and substituting back in for u gives \frac{-1}{64} \ln(\cos(-8 x))+C Combining it with the non-integrated term from integration by parts, we get the final answer: \int x \sec^{2}\mathopen{}\left(-8x\right) \, dx = \frac{1}{-8} x \tan(-8 x) - \frac{-1}{64} \ln(\cos(-8 x))+C

statement.p: Use integration by parts to evaluate the integral.
If g(1)=1, g(5)=-5, and \displaystyle \int_1^5 \! g(x) \, dx = -10, evaluate the integral \displaystyle \int_1^5 \! x g'(x)\, dx.
Answer:

solution.p: SOLUTION

Let u = x, \; dv = g'(x) \, dx \; \Rightarrow \; du = dx, \; v = g(x). We then have \int_1^5 \! x g'(x)\, dx = \Big[x g(x)\Big]_1^5 - \int_1^5 g(x) \, dx = \Big[ 5\cdot g(5) - 1 \cdot g(1) \Big] + 10 = 5\cdot (-5) - 1 + 10 = -16

statement.p: For each of the indefinite integrals below, the main question is to decide whether the integral can be evaluated using a basic antiderivative, u-substitution, integration by parts, a combination of u-substitution and integration by parts, or none of these other techniques.
For integrals for which your answer is affirmative (u-sub, by parts, combo), you should be able to state what u and du are, or what u and dv are.
Calculate the integral below by partial fractions and by using the indicated substitution. Be sure that you can show how the results you obtain are the same. \int \frac{2x}{x^{2}-1}\,dx
First, rewrite this with partial fractions:
\int \frac{2x}{x^{2}-1}\,dx = \int dx + \int dx = + + C.

p.em: (Note that you should not include the +C in your entered answer, as it has been provided at the end of the expression.)

statement.p: Next, use the substitution w = x^2 - 1 to find the integral:
\int \frac{2x}{x^{2}-1}\,dx = \int dw = + C = + C.

p.em: (For the second answer blank, give your antiderivative in terms of the variable w. Again, note that you should not include the +C in your answer.)

static.solution:
\frac{2x}{x^2-1}=\frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{x-1} so that 2x = A(x-1)+B(x+1) = (A+B)x + 1 (-A+B). Solving, we get A=B=1, so that \int \frac{2x}{x^2-1}\,dx= \int \left(\frac{1}{x+1}+\frac{1}{x-1}\right)\,dx =\ln|x+1|+\ln|x-1|+C.
Using the substitution w=x^2-1, we get dw= 2x\,dx, so we have \int \frac{2x}{x^2-1}\,dx= \int \frac{dw}{w}=\ln|w|+C = \ln|x^2-1|+C.
The properties of logarithms show that the two results are the same: \ln|x+1|+\ln|x-1| = \ln|(x+1)(x-1)| =\ln|x^2-1|.

static.solution: \frac{3 x + 2}{x^2-3x+2} = \frac{3 x+2}{(x-1)(x-2)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x-2}. Multiplying by (x-1) and (x-2), this becomes 3 x+2 = A(x-2)+B(x-1), or A+B = 3 \quad\hbox{and}\quad -2A - B = 2. Solving this system yields A = -5 and B = 8. solution.p: SOLUTION

Multiplying by the least common denominator gives 4x^{2}+2x+54 = A(x^2+9)+(Bx+C)(x - 1) Rearranging terms on the right hand side, yields 4x^{2}+2x+54 = (A+B)x^2+(-B+C)x + 9 A - C Now we equate the coefficients: \begin{array}{rl} A+B \amp = 4 \\ -B +C \amp = 2 \\ 9 A - C \amp = 54 \end{array} Solving the system gives A=6, \; B = -2 and C= 0 so the partial fraction decomposition is \frac{4x^{2}+2x+54}{(x - 1)(x^2+9)} = \frac{6}{x - 1} + \frac{-2x}{x^2+9} The definite integral is then \displaystyle \int \frac{4x^{2}+2x+54}{(x - 1)(x^2+9)} dx = 6\ln\mathopen{}\left(\left|x-1\right|\right) - 1\ln\mathopen{}\left(x^{2}+9\right) +C

statement.p: (a) What is the exact value of \int_{0}^{6}\,e^x\,dx?
Find LEFT(2), RIGHT(2), TRAP(2), MID(2), and SIMP(4); compute the error for each.
Repeat part (b) with n=4 (instead of n=2).

static.solution:
(a) \int_{0}^{6}\,e^x\,dx = e^x\bigg|_{0}^{6} = e^6 - e^0 \approx 402.4288\ldots
(b) Computing the sums directly, since \Delta x=3, we have
LEFT(2) = 3\cdot e^0 + 3\cdot e^{3} \approx 63.2567
RIGHT(2) = 3\cdot e^{3} + 3\cdot e^{6} \approx 1270.54
TRAP(2) = \frac 1 2 ( 63.2567 + 1270.54 ) \approx 666.9
MID(2) = 3\cdot e^{1.5} + 3\cdot e^{3\cdot 1.5} \approx 283.497
and SIMP(4) = (2 MID(2) + TRAP(2))/3 \approx 411.297.
And the errors are just the actual value minus the approximate values, or
error(LEFT(2)) = 339.172; error(RIGHT(2)) = -868.111; error(TRAP(2)) = -264.471; error(MID(2)) = 118.933; and error(SIMP(4)) = -8.868.
(c) Similarly, since \Delta x = 0.75, we have
LEFT(4) = 173.377; error = 229.052
RIGHT(4) = 777.02; error = -374.591
TRAP(4) = 475.198; error = -72.769
MID(4) = 367.038; error = 35.391
SIMP(8) = 403.091; error = -0.662.
(d) For LEFT and RIGHT, we expect the error to go down by 1/2, and this is very roughly what we see. For MID and TRAP, we expect the error to go down by 1/4, and this is approximately what we see. For SIMP, we expect the error to go down by 1/16, again as observed.

Find the area between y = 6 \sin x and y = 7 \cos x over the interval \left[0,\pi\right]. Sketch the curves if necessary.

static.solution:
Over the interval [0,\pi], the graphs y = 6\sin x and y = 7 \cos x intersect when 6\sin x = 7 \cos x, i.e., \tan x = \frac{7}{6}, i.e., x=\tan^{-1}(\frac{7}{6})=0.862170054667226.
Let t = \tan^{-1}(\frac{7}{6}).
Over the interval \left[0, t\right], the graph of y = 6\sin x lies below that of y = 7 \cos x. Hence, the area between the two curves is \int_0^{ t}(7 \cos x-6 \sin x)dx \begin{array}{ll} \amp =\left.(7\sin x+6\cos x)\right|_0^{ t} \cr \amp =\left(7\sin t+6\cos t\right)-(7\cdot 0+6\cdot 1)\cr \amp =\left(7\sin t+6\cos t\right)-6 \end{array}
Since t = \tan^{-1}(\frac{7}{6}), we have \tan t = \frac{7}{6}. Considering a rightangle triangle with an angle which opposite side has length 7 and adjacent side has length 6, we see that the hypotenues is \sqrt{85}. Thus \sin t = \frac{7}{\sqrt{85}} and \cos t = \frac{6}{\sqrt{85}}.
7\sin t+6\cos t = \frac{7^2}{\sqrt{85}} + \frac{6^2}{\sqrt{85}} = \frac{7^2+6^2}{\sqrt{85}} = \frac{85}{\sqrt{85}}=\sqrt{85}.
Thus, \int_0^{ t}(7 \cos x-6 \sin x)dx= \sqrt{85}-6.
Over the interval \left[ t,\pi\right], the graph of y = 6\sin x lies above that of y = 7 \cos x. Hence, the area between the two curves is \int^\pi_{ t}(6\sin x - 7 \cos x)dx \begin{array}{ll} \amp =-\left.(7\sin x+6\cos x)\right|^\pi_{ t} \cr \amp =6 + \sqrt{85} \end{array}
Thus the total area is the sum of the above two integrals, which is 2\sqrt{85}.

statement.p: A rod has length 5 meters. At a distance x meters from its left end, the density of the rod is given by \delta(x)=5 + 5 x g/m.
(a) Complete the Riemann sum for the total mass of the rod (use Dx in place of \Delta x):
mass = \Sigma
(b) Convert the Riemann sum to an integral and find the exact mass.
mass =
(include )

static.solution:
(a) Suppose we choose an x, 0\leq x\leq 5. If \Delta x is a small fraction of a meter, then the density of the rod is approximately \delta(x) anywhere from x to x+\Delta x meters from the left end of the rod. The mass of the rod from x to x+\Delta x meters is therefore approximately \delta(x) \Delta x = (5 + 5 x)\Delta x. If we slice the rod into N pieces, then a Riemann sum is \Sigma_{i=1}^{N}(5 + 5 x_i)\Delta x, or, more loosely, \Sigma (5 + 5 x)\Delta x.

statement.p: Suppose that the density of cars (in cars per mile) down a 20-mile stretch of the Pennsylvania Turnpike is approximated by \delta(x) = 275 \left(2+\sin\left(4\sqrt{x + 0.2}\right)\right), at a distance x miles from the Breezewood toll plaza. Sketch a graph of this function for 0\leq x\leq 20.
(a) Complete the Riemann sum that approximates the total number of cars on this 20-mile stretch (use Dx instead of \Delta x):
Number = \Sigma
(b) Find the total number of cars on the 20-mile stretch.
Number =

static.solution:
(a) Suppose we choose an x, 0\le x\le 20. We approximate the density of the number of the cars between x and x+\Delta x miles as \delta(x) cars per mile. Therefore, the number of cars between x and x+\Delta x is approximately \delta(x)\Delta x. If we slice the 20 mile strip into N slices, we get that the total number of cars is C \approx \Sigma_{i=1}^N \delta(x_i)\Delta x = \Sigma_{i=1}^N \left[ 550 + 275\sin(4\sqrt{x_i + 0.2})\right]\Delta x, where \Delta x =20/N. This is a right-hand approximation; the corresponding left-hand approximation is \Sigma_{i=0}^{N-1}\delta(x_i)\Delta x. We can more loosely write both approximations without referring to the number of steps as C \approx \Sigma \left[ 550 + 275\sin(4\sqrt{x + 0.2})\right]\Delta x.
(b) As N\to\infty, the Riemann sum above approaches the integral C =\int_0^{20} (550 + 275\sin4\sqrt{x + 0.2})\,dx. If we calculate the integral numerically, we find C\approx 10529.2. We can also find the integral exactly as follows: C = \int_0^{20} (550 + 275\sin4\sqrt{x +0.2})\,dx = \int_0^{20} 550\,dx +\int_0^{20} 275\sin4\sqrt{x + 0.2}\,dx = 11000 + 275\int_0^{20}\sin4\sqrt{x +0.2}\,dx. Let w = \sqrt{x +0.2}, so x =w^2 -0.2 and dx =2w\,dw. Then \int_{x=0}^{x=20}\sin 4\sqrt{x +0.2}\,dx = 2\int_{w=\sqrt{0.2}}^{w=\sqrt{20.2}} w\sin 4w\,dw, = 2\left[-{1\over 4}w\cos 4w +{1\over 16}\sin 4w\right] \bigg|_{\sqrt{0.2}}^{\sqrt{20.2}} \approx -1.597. (To find the integral we used the appropriate entry in a table of integrals.) Using this, we have C\approx 11000 + 275(-1.597) \approx 10529.2, which matches our numerical approximation.

statement.p: A tank in the shape of an inverted right circular cone has height 6 meters and radius 2 meters. It is filled with 5 meters of hot chocolate. Find the work required to empty the tank by pumping the hot chocolate over the top of the tank. The density of hot chocolate is \delta = 1030 \ \textrm{kg}/\textrm{m}^3. Your answer must include the correct .
Work =

solution.p: SOLUTION

We think of the tank as made from infinitely many 'infinitesimal' horizontal slices, with x the vertical distance an infinitesimal slice of the water is from the bottom of the tank (the vertex of the right circular cone).
A cross section through the vertical center to the side is approximated below (not necessarily to scale).

Now the large right triangle with height 6 and top side length 2 is similar to the right triangle with height x and top side length r. So \frac{6}{2} = \frac{x}{r}\implies 6 r = 2 x or r = {\frac{1}{3}} x.
Therefore the area of every infinitesimal slice is A(x) = \pi(r)^2=\pi({\frac{1}{3}} x)^2={\frac{1}{9}} \pi x^2 \text{meter}^2.

The infinitesimal slice has volume dV=A(x)dx = {\frac{1}{9}} \pi x^2\,dx \text{meter}^3, and since mass = density\times volume, the mass of our infinitesimal slice is dm = \delta dV where \delta= 1030 \frac{kg}{\text{meter}^3}.
So the mass of the slice at x is \delta\,dV= (1030)\left({\frac{1}{9}} \pi x^2\right)\,dx kg. We now must find mgh for each slice.
Each slice at x must be lifted a height h = (6-x) meters, and g=9.8 \frac{meters}{sec^2} . So mgh for each slice is 9.8(1030)\left({\frac{1}{9}} \pi x^2\right)(6-x)\,dx Joules.

statement.p: A rectangular swimming pool 60 ft long, 10 ft wide, and 16 ft deep is filled with water to a depth of 14 ft. Use an integral to find the work required to pump all the water out over the top. (Take as the density of water \delta = 62.4 \hbox{lb/ft}^3.)
Work =
(include )

static.solution:
h ft above the bottom, a slice of thickness \Delta h has \hbox{Volume }\approx 60\cdot 10\Delta h \hbox{ ft}{}^3. Since the density of water is \rho lb/ft{}^3, \hbox{Weight of the slice }\approx\rho(60 \cdot 10 \cdot \Delta h) \hbox{ lbs}. The distance to lift the slice of water at height h ft is 16 - h ft, so the work to move one slice, \Delta W, is \Delta W = \rho \cdot \hbox{Volume} \cdot \hbox{Distance lifted} \approx \rho(60 \cdot 10 \cdot \Delta h)(16 - h) = 600 \rho (16 - h) \Delta h\hbox{ ft-lb}.
The work done, W, to pump all the water is the sum of the work done on the pieces: W \approx \Sigma\, 600 \rho(16-h)\Delta h. As \Delta h \rightarrow 0, we obtain a definite integral. Since h varies from h = 0 to h = 14 and \rho=62.4\hbox{ lb/ft}{}^3, the total work is: W = \int_0^{14} 37440 (16-h)dh = 37440 \left(16 h - {h^2\over 2}\right)\bigg|_0^{14} = 37440 (126) = 4717440\, \hbox{lbf}.

statement.p: Water in a cylinder of height 12 ft and radius 3 ft is to be pumped out. The density of water is 62.4 lb/ft{}^3. Find the work required if

static.solution:
(a) We slice the water horizontally. Each slice is a cylindrical slab of radius and thickness \Delta h, so
\hbox{Volume of each slab }\approx \pi 3^2 \Delta h\hbox{ ft}^3. The density of water is \delta = 62.4 lb/ft{}^3, so \hbox{Weight of slab }\approx \delta\pi3^2 \Delta h \hbox{ lb.} Water at a height of h ft must be lifted a distance of 12 - h ft. \hbox{ Work to move one slice} =\delta \cdot \hbox{Volume} \cdot \hbox{Distance lifted} \approx \delta (\pi (3)^2 \Delta h)(12 - h)\hbox{ ft-lb.} Plugging in \delta=62.4 and since h varies from h = 0 to h = 12, the total work, W, is: W = \int_0^{12}{\delta(\pi 3^2 )(12-h)dh} = 3^2\delta \pi \int_0^{12}{(12 - h)dh} = (3^2) 62.4 \pi\left(12 h-\frac{h^2}2\right) \Bigg|_0^{12} = 127031\ {\rm lbf}. The total work required is 127031\ {\rm lbf}.
(b) This is the same as part (a) except the water must be lifted a distance of 18 - h ft. The total work is: W = \int_0^{12}{\delta(\pi 3^2 )(6-h)dh} = 3^2\delta \pi \int_0^{12}{(18 - h)dh} = (3^2) 62.4 \pi \left(18 h-\frac{h^2}2\right)\Bigg|_0^{12} = 254062\ {\rm lbf}. The total work required is 254062\ {\rm lbf}.
(c) This is the same as part (a) except that h varies from h=0 to h=7. The total work is: W = \int_0^{7}{\delta(\pi 3^2 )(12-h)dh} = 3^2\delta \pi \int_0^{7}{(12 -h)dh} = (3^2) 62.4 \pi \left(12 h-\frac{h^2}2\right)\Bigg|_0^{12} = 104977\ {\rm lbf}. The total work required is 104977\ {\rm lbf}.

static.solution: \int_{0}^{\infty} 4x^{2}e^{-x^{3}} dx = \lim_{b \rightarrow \infty} \int_{0}^b 4x^{2}e^{-x^{3}} dx = \left.\lim_{b \rightarrow \infty} \left({{-4} \over 3} e^{-x^3}\right) \right|_0^b = \lim_{b \rightarrow \infty} \left({{-4} \over 3} e^{-b^3} - {{-4} \over 3} e^{-0^3}\right) = 0 + {4\over 3} e^{-0} = {4\over 3} . This integral converges to {4\over 3}.

statement.p: Calculate the integral, if it converges. If it diverges, enter diverges for your answer.

static.solution: 1/v is undefined at v=0. To evaluate it, we must split the region of integration up into two pieces, from 0 to 4 and from -4 to 0. But notice, \int_0^{4}{1\over v}\, dv = \lim_{b\to 0^+}\int_b^{4} {1\over v}\, dv = \lim_{b\to 0^+}\left({\ln v}\bigg|_b^{4}\right) = \ln(4) - \ln b. As b\to 0^+, this goes to infinity and the integral diverges, so our original integral also diverges.

statement.p: Find the area under the curve y = {\cos(t)\over\sin(t)} between t = 0 and t = \pi/2. Enter diverges if the area is not bounded.
area =

static.solution:
\int_0^{\pi/2}\,{\cos(t)\over\sin(t)}\,dt. However, the integrand is undefined at t = 0, so this is an improper integral. We find \int_0^{\pi/2}\,{\cos(t)\over\sin(t)}\,dt = \lim\limits_{a\to0^{+}}\,\int_a^{\pi/2}\,{\cos(t)\over\sin(t)}\,dt = \lim\limits_{a\to0^{+}}\,(\ln|\sin(t)|)\bigg|_a^{\pi/2} = \lim\limits_{a\to0^{+}} ( \ln(1) - \ln|\sin(a)| ). However, -\ln|\sin(a)| is undefined as a\to0, so this integral diverges.
Thus, because the integral diverges, the area is not bounded.

solution.p: Substitute x = r \tan{\theta}, so that

Then since x = r \tan{\theta} = r \displaystyle\frac{\sin{\theta}}{\cos{\theta}} we see \sin{\theta} = \displaystyle\frac{x}{r}\cos{\theta} = \displaystyle\frac{x}{r\sec{\theta}} = \displaystyle\frac{x}{r\sqrt{1+ \tan^2{\theta}}} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{r^2 + x^2}}

static.solution: y, we can compute the slope of the tangent line using the formula for dy/dt. So given a value of t, we must first compute (or approximate) a value of y. When t=0, the initial condition tells us that y=0, so the corresponding slope is \frac{1}{2}(0+1) = \frac{1}{2} and the equation of the tangent line is y=\frac{1}{2}t. statement.p: Use Euler's method to solve \frac{dB}{dt}= 0.08 B with initial value B=1500 when t=0 .
A. \Delta t = 1 and 1 step: B(1) \approx
B. \Delta t = 0.5 and 2 steps: B(1) \approx
C. \Delta t = 0.25 and 4 steps: B(1) \approx

D. Suppose B is the balance in a bank account earning interest. Be sure that you can explain why the result of your calculation in part (a) is equivalent to compounding the interest once a year instead of continuously. Then interpret the result of your calculations in parts (b) and (c) in terms of compound interest.

static.solution:
A. With one step of \Delta t = 1, we have
B(1) \approx 1500 + (1)(0.08)(1500) = 1620.
B. With two steps of \Delta t = 0.5, we have
B(0.5) \approx 1500 + (0.5)(0.08)(1500) = 1560,
B(1) \approx 1560 + (0.5)(0.08)(1560) = 1622.4.
Note that we can simplify this some: B(0.5) \approx (1 + \frac{0.08}{2}) (1500), so that B(1) \approx B(0.5) + \frac{0.08}{2} B(0.5) = (1 + \frac{0.08}{2})^2 (1500).
C. With four steps of \Delta t = 0.25, we have, following the pattern we saw in (B),
B(0.25) \approx 1500 + (0.25)(0.08)(1500) = (1 + \frac{0.08}{4}) (1500),
B(0.5) \approx B(0.25) + (0.25)(0.08) B(0.25) = (1 + \frac{0.08}{4})^2 (1500),
B(0.75) \approx B(0.5) + (0.25)(0.08) B(0.5) = (1 + \frac{0.08}{4})^3 (1500), and B(1) \approx B(0.75) + (0.25)(0.08) B(0.75) = (1 + \frac{0.08}{4})^4 (1500) = 1623.648.
D. In part (A), we get our approximation by making a single increment, \Delta B, where \Delta B is just 0.08 B. If we think in terms of interest, \Delta B is just like getting one end of the year interest payment. Since \Delta B is 0.08 times the balance B, it is like getting 120 dollars.
Part (B) is equivalent to computing the final amount in an account that begins with 1500 dollars and earns 120 dollars twice annually. Each step is like computing the interest after 6 months. When t=0.5, for example, the interest is \Delta B=(0.08 B)\cdot\frac{1}{2}, and we add this to 1500 dollars to get the new balance.
Similarly, part (C) is equivalent to the final amount in an account that has an initial balance of 1500 dollars and earns 120 dollars compounded quarterly.

statement.p: Find the solution to the differential equation \frac{dy}{dt} = 0.7 (y - 200) if y=75 when t=0.

static.solution: \int\frac{dy}{y-200} = \int 0.7 dt, so \ln|y-200| = 0.7 t +C. Solving for y, y = 200 + A e^{0.7 t}, where A = \pm e^C. The initial condition, y(0)=75, gives 75 = 200 + A, so A = 125, and y= 200 - 125 e^{0.7 t}.

statement.p: Find the solution to the differential equation \frac{dy}{dt} = y^2(7 + t), y=3 when t=1.

static.solution: \frac{dy}{y^2} = (7 + t)\,dt, so \int \frac{dy}{y^2} = \int (7 + t)\,dt, and -\frac{1}{y} = {1\over2}(7 + t)^2 + C, giving y=-\frac{2}{(7 + t)^2 + A}, where A = 2C. Since y=3 when t=1, we have 3 = -\frac{2}{8^2 + A},\quad \hbox{ so } \quad 3 A + 192 = -2, and A = -{{194\over3}}. Thus y = -\frac{2}{(7 + t)^2 - {{194\over3}}}.

static.solution:
Thus we get different solution behaviors for the initial conditions P(0) = 1, P(0) > 1, and 0 \lt P(0) \lt 1. The initial condition P(0) = 0 gives the zero solution, which is an equilibrium and has the same behavior as the initial condition P(0) = 1. Note that we can also say that the behavior for initial conditions 0 \lt P(0) \lt 0.5 is different from that for initial conditions 0.5 \le P(0) \lt 1, because the former will be sigmoidal while the latter are strictly exponential.
From the solutions graphed above, or by looking at the slope field, we can see that the equilibrium solution P = 1 is stable. The other equilibrium solution, P = 0 is unstable.
Also by looking at the solution curves, we can see that P is increasing when 0 \lt P \lt 1 and decreasing when P > 1. In the long run, we're most likely to start with a non-zero population and thus P\to 1. The solution curves with initial populations of less than P= 0.5 have inflection points at P=0.5. (This will be demonstrated algebraically below.) At the inflection point, the population is growing fastest.
A graph of dP/dt against P is shown below.
Since \frac{dP}{dt}=2 P - 2 P^2 = 2 P(1 - P), the graph of \frac{dP}{dt} against P is a parabola, opening downward with P intercepts at 0 and 1. The quantity \frac{dP}{dt} is positive for 0 \lt P \lt 1, negative for P > 1 (and P \lt 0). The quantity \frac{dP}{dt} is 0 at P=0 and P=, and maximum at P=0.5. The fact that \frac{dP}{dt} =0 at P=0 and P=1 tells us that these are equilibria. Further, since \frac{dP}{dt}> 0 for 0 \lt P \lt 1, we see that solution curves starting here will increase toward P=1.
If the population starts at a value P\lt 0.5, it increases at an increasing rate up to P=0.5. After this, P continues to increase, but at a decreasing rate. The fact that \frac{dP}{dt} has a maximum at P=0.5 tells us that there is a point of inflection when P=0.5. Similarly, since \frac{dP}{dt} \lt 0 for P > 1, solution curves starting with P > 1 will decrease to P = 1. Thus, P=1 is a stable equilibrium.

statement.p: The total number of people infected with a virus often grows like a logistic curve. Suppose that 15 people originally have the virus, and that in the early stages of the virus (with time, t, measured in weeks), the number of people infected is increasing exponentially with k=1.9. It is estimated that, in the long run, approximately 7000 people become infected.
(a) Use this information to find a logistic function to model this situation.

(b) Sketch a graph of your answer to part (a). Use your graph to estimate the length of time until the rate at which people are becoming infected starts to decrease. What is the vertical coordinate at this point?
vertical coordinate =

static.solution:
(a) We know that a logistic curve can be modeled by the function P=\frac{L}{1+Ce^{-kt}} where C=(L-P_0)/P_0 and P is the number of people infected by the virus at a particular time t. We know that L is the limiting value, or the maximal number of people infected with the virus, so in our case L=7000. We are also told that initially there are only 15 people infected with the virus so that we get P_0=15. Thus we have C = \frac{L-P_0}{P_0} = \frac{7000-15}{15} = 465.666666666667. We are also told that in the early stages of the virus, infection grows exponentially with k=1.9. Thus we get that the logistic function for people infected is P=\frac{7000}{1+465.666666666667 e^{-1.9 t}}.
(b) Graphing this solution, we see
Looking at the graph we see that the the point at which the rate changes from increasing to decreasing, the inflection point, occurs at roughly t=3.25 giving a value of P=3625. Thus after roughly 3625 people have been infected, the rate of infection starts dropping.

statement.p: (b) Use this graph to sketch the shape of solution curves with various initial values: use your answers in part (a), and where dP/dt is increasing and decreasing to decide what the shape of the curves has to be. Based on your solution curves, why is P=b/a called the threshold population?
If P(0) > b/a, what happens to P in the long run?
If P(0) = b/a, what happens to P in the long run?
If P(0) \lt b/a, what happens to P in the long run?

static.solution:
(a) A graph of dP/dt vs P is shown below.
Thus, dP/dt is negative when 0 \lt P \lt b/a and positive when b/a \lt P \lt \infty (we ignore P \lt 0, because this doesn't make sense for a population).
(b)
We can see from the graph above that P is a decreasing function when P\lt \frac{b}{a}. Similarly, when P>\frac{b}{a}, the sign of dP/dt is positive, so P is an increasing function. Thus solution curves starting above \frac{b}{a} are increasing, and those starting below \frac{b}{a} are decreasing.
We can also see that for P>\frac{b}{a}, the slope, \frac{dP}{dt}, increases with P, so the graph of P against t is concave up. For 0\lt P\lt \frac{b}{a}, the value of P decreases with time. As P decreases, the slope \frac{dP}{dt} decreases for \frac{b}{2a}\lt P\lt \frac{b}{a}, and increases toward 0 for 0\lt P\lt \frac{b}{2a}. Thus solution curves starting just below the threshold value of \frac{b}{a} are concave down for \frac{b}{2a}\lt P\lt \frac{b}{a} and concave up and asymptotic to the t-axis for 0\lt P\lt \frac{b}{2a}. Thus, solution curves are similar to those shown in the graph below
P=\frac{b}{a} is called the threshold population because for populations greater than \frac{b}{a}, the population will increase without bound. For populations less than \frac{b}{a}, the population will go to zero, i.e. to extinction. The value \frac{b}{a} is an unstable equilibrium, and P=0 is a stable equilibrium.

statement.p: Calculate the Taylor polynomials T_2(x) and T_3(x) centered at x = \frac{\pi }{6} for f(x) = \sin\mathopen{}\left(x\right).

static.solution:
\begin{array}{lcll} T(x) \amp = \amp \amp f(a) \cr\cr \amp \amp + \amp \frac{f'(a)}{1!} (x-a) \cr \cr \amp \amp + \amp \frac{f''(a)}{2!} (x-a)^2 \cr \cr \amp \amp + \amp \ldots \cr \cr \amp \amp + \amp \frac{f^n(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n \end{array}
So, in this case, f(x) = \sin\mathopen{}\left(x\right) and
T_2(x) = A + B(x-\frac{\pi }{6}) + C(x-\frac{\pi }{6})^2
where
A=f(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}=0.5
B=f'(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=0.866025403784439
C=\frac{f''(\frac{\pi }{6})}{2!}=-\frac{1}{4}=-0.25
Thus,
T_2(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} (x - \frac{\pi }{6}) - \frac{1}{4} (x - \frac{\pi }{6})^2
or
T_2(x) = 0.5+0.866025\mathopen{}\left(x-\frac{\pi }{6}\right)-0.25\mathopen{}\left(x-\frac{\pi }{6}\right)^{2}
Similarly,
T_3(x) = D + E(x-\frac{\pi }{6}) + F(x-\frac{\pi }{6})^2 + G(x-\frac{\pi }{6})^3
where
D=f(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2} = 0.5
E=f'(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} =0.866025403784439
F=\frac{f''(\frac{\pi }{6})}{2!}=-\frac{1}{4} =-0.25
G=\frac{f'''(\frac{\pi }{6})}{3!}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{12}=-0.144337567297406
Thus, T_3(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} (x - \frac{\pi }{6}) - \frac{1}{4} (x - \frac{\pi }{6})^2 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{12} (x - \frac{\pi }{6})^3
or
T_3(x) = 0.5+0.866025\mathopen{}\left(x-\frac{\pi }{6}\right)-0.25\mathopen{}\left(x-\frac{\pi }{6}\right)^{2}-0.144338\mathopen{}\left(x-\frac{\pi }{6}\right)^{3}

statement.p: Suppose g is a function which has continuous derivatives, and that g(7)=4, g'(7)=1, g''(7)=5, g'''(7)=-4.

With T_3, g(6.9)\approx

static.solution:
g(x) = g(7) + g'(7)(x-7) + \frac{g''(7)}{2!}(x-7)^2 +\frac{g'''(7)}{3!}(x-7)^3+\cdots Substituting gives g(x) = 4 + 1(x-7) + \frac{5}{2!}(x-7)^2 +\frac{-4}{3!}(x-7)^3+\cdots
(a) The degree 2 Taylor polynomial, T_2 (x), is obtained by truncating after the (x-7)^2 term: T_2(x) = 4+1\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)^{2}.
(b) The degree 3 Taylor polynomial, T_3 (x), is obtained by truncating after the (x-7)^3 term: T_3 (x) = 4+1\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}\mathopen{}\left(-4\right)\mathopen{}\left(x-7\right)^{3}
(c) Substitute x=6.9 into the Taylor polynomial of degree 2: T_2(4.9) = 4+1\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)^{2} = 3.925. From the Taylor polynomial of degree 3, we obtain T_3(4.9) = 4+1\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}\mathopen{}\left(-4\right)\mathopen{}\left(6.9-7\right)^{3} = 3.92567.

\cos(x) and its first three derivatives are

static.solution:
(a) Since 1 - x + x^2 - x^3 + \cdots is a geometric series with base - x, we know its sum: 1 - x + x^2 - x^3 + \cdots = \frac{1}{1 + x} = 0.8. Solving for x, we get x = \frac{1}{4}.
(b) Similarly, since x - \frac{x^3}{3!} + \frac{x^5}{5!} - \cdots is the Taylor series for \sin(x), we know its sum as well: x - \frac{x^3}{3!} + \frac{x^5}{5!} - \cdots = \sin(x) = 0.8. Solving for x, we get x = \arcsin(0.8).

statement.p: Use the ratio test to find the open interval of convergence of \sum_{n=1}^\infty\,{n^3\,x^{3 n}\over 5^{3 n}}.
interval of convergence =

p.em: (Enter your answer as an interval: thus, if the interval of convergence were -3 \lt x\lt 5, you would enter (-3,5). Use Inf for any endpoint at infinity.)

solution.p: We use the ratio test: \left|{a_{n+1} \over {a_n}}\right| = \left|{{(n+1)^3 x^{3(n+1)}} \over {5^{3(n+1)}}} \cdot {{5^{3 n}} \over {n^3 x^{3 n}}}\right| = \left({{n+1} \over n}\right)^2 \cdot {{x^3} \over 125}. Since {{(n+1)}/ n} \rightarrow 1 as n \rightarrow \infty, we have \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|{{a_{n+1}} \over {a_n}}\right|={{x^3}\over 125}. We have {{x^3}/ 125} \lt 1 when |x| \lt 5. The radius of convergence is 5 and the series converges for -5 \lt x \lt 5. (And we don't know what happens at x=2 or x=-2.)

static.solution:
\displaystyle \frac{3}{1-6 x} = 3 \cdot \sum_{n=0}^\infty (6 x)^n. Then we can see that c_n = 3 \cdot 6^n, making c_0 = 3, c_1 = 3 \cdot 6 = 18, c_2 = 3 \cdot 6^2 = 108, etc.
Regarding the radius of convergence, we perform the standard ratio test: \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{3(6 x)^{n+1}}{3(6 x)^n} \right| = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| 6 x \right| = \left| 6 x \right| And then \left| 6 x \right| \lt 1 \iff \left| x \right| \lt \frac 1 {6}, making R = \frac 1 {6}.

solution.p: SOLUTION
The n^{th} degree approximation of f(1.07) about x=1 is given by:
Therefore,
f''(x) is always positive in the interval [1,1.07] so T_{2}(1.07) is a overestimate of f(1.07).

static.solution:
Ax^n the antiderivative is just the term whose derivative is Ax^n. That is, \frac{A}{n+1}x^{n+1} + C where C is an unknown constant. Also, recall that the antiderivative of the \sec^2 function is the \tan function. Applying these rules term-by-term to our function, we get:
F(t) = 4\tan{t} - \frac{9}{3}t^{3} + C \quad = 4\tan{t} - 3t^{3} + C
Where C is an artibrary constant. We are further told that F(0) = 0 so plugging this into the above general antiderivative, we get:
F(0) = 4\tan{0} - 3(0)^{3} + C = 0
So that the specific antiderivative is: F(t) = 4\tan{t} - 3t^{3}

statement.p: For each of the indefinite integrals below, decide whether the integral can be evaluated: immediately because it's a basic integral, using u-substitution, integration by parts, with multiple techniques, or if none of those will work.

hint.p: Note that \displaystyle \frac{2x+3}{1+x^2} can be rewritten as \displaystyle \frac{2x}{1+x^2} +\frac{3}{1+x^2}.

solution.p: \displaystyle \int \frac{1}{1+x^2} \, dx = \arctan(x)+C, a basic integral rule.

\displaystyle \int \frac{x}{1+x^2} \, dx can be solved with u-substitution, letting u=1+x^2 so that du = 2x \, dx, which turns the integral into \displaystyle \frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u} \, du, which we can integrate.

\displaystyle \int \frac{2x+3}{1+x^2} \, dx The substitution from the previous problem doesn't cancel out the 2x+3. We could split the integral up into \displaystyle \int \frac{2x}{1+x^2} \, dx + \int \frac{3}{1+x^2} \, dx, and the first is u-sub, while the second is a basic integral involving \arctan (x) OR, we could do integration by parts twice. The first time, let u=2x+3 while dv = \frac{1}{1+x^2} \, dx, which gets us an answer involving \displaystyle \int \arctan(x) \, dx, which can itself be done with integration by parts, letting u= \arctan(x) and dv=dx, giving an integral of \displaystyle \int \frac{x}{1+x^2} \, dx, which is solved with u-sub.

\displaystyle \int \frac{e^x}{1+(e^x)^2} \, dx can be solved with u-substitution, letting u=e^x so that du = e^x \, dx, which turns the integral into \displaystyle \int \frac{1}{1+u^2} \, du, which integrates to \arctan(u).
\displaystyle \int \frac{1}{x^2-1} \, dx can't be done with u-sub or integration by parts, and it's not basic.

Calculate the integral below by partial fractions and by using the indicated substitution. Be sure that you can show how the results you obtain are the same. \int \frac{2x}{x^{2}-36}\,dx
First, rewrite this with partial fractions:
\int \frac{2x}{x^{2}-36}\,dx = \int dx + \int dx = + + C.

p.em: (Note that you should not include the +C in your entered answer, as it has been provided at the end of the expression.)

statement.p: Next, use the substitution w = x^2 - 36 to find the integral:
\int \frac{2x}{x^{2}-36}\,dx = \int dw = + C = + C.

p.em: (For the second answer blank, give your antiderivative in terms of the variable w. Again, note that you should not include the +C in your answer.)

static.solution:
\frac{2x}{x^2-36}=\frac{A}{x+6}+\frac{B}{x-6} so that 2x = A(x-6)+B(x+6) = (A+B)x + 6 (-A+B). Solving, we get A=B=1, so that \int \frac{2x}{x^2-36}\,dx= \int \left(\frac{1}{x+6}+\frac{1}{x-6}\right)\,dx =\ln|x+6|+\ln|x-6|+C.
Using the substitution w=x^2-36, we get dw= 2x\,dx, so we have \int \frac{2x}{x^2-36}\,dx= \int \frac{dw}{w}=\ln|w|+C = \ln|x^2-36|+C.
The properties of logarithms show that the two results are the same: \ln|x+6|+\ln|x-6| = \ln|(x+6)(x-6)| =\ln|x^2-36|.

hint.p: The integral involves \sin u and \cos u where the exponent of \cos u is an odd, positive integer, namely, 3. So we factor out a copy of \cos(13 x) and use the identity \sin^2 u + \cos^2 u = 1 to turn the remaining \cos^2(13 x) into an expression involving \sin^2(13 x).

Thus the integral can be rewritten as \int \sin^{12}\mathopen{}\left(13x\right)\cos^{3}\mathopen{}\left(13x\right) \, dx = \int \sin^{12} (13 x) \cos^2(13 x) \cos(13 x) \, dx = \int \sin^{12} (13 x) \bigg(1-\sin^2(13 x)\bigg) \cos(13 x) \, dx and we use u-substitution.
Letting u= \sin (13 x) so du = 13 \cos (13 x) \, dx and thus \displaystyle dx = \frac{ du}{13 \cos (13 x)}.

This turns the integral into \int u^{12} (1-u^2) \cos(13 x) \, \frac{ du}{13 \cos (13 x)} = \frac{1}{13}\int u^{12} (1-u^2) \, du which can be multiplied out, and then each part integrated by power rule.

solution.p: We factor out a copy of \cos(13 x) and use the identity \sin^2 u + \cos^2 u = 1 to turn the remaining \cos^2(13 x) into an expression involving \sin^2(13 x).
Then we use u-substitution, letting u= \sin (13 x) so du = 13 \cos (13 x) \, dx and thus \displaystyle dx = \frac{ du}{13 \cos (13 x)}.

p.me: \begin{aligned} \int \sin^{12}\mathopen{}\left(13x\right)\cos^{3}\mathopen{}\left(13x\right) \, dx \amp = \int \sin^{12} (13 x) \cos^2(13 x) \cos(13 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = \int \sin^{12} (13 x) \bigg(1-\sin^2(13 x)\bigg) \cos(13 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = \int u^{12} (1-u^2) \cos(13 x) \, \frac{ du}{13 \cos (13 x)} \\\\ \amp = \frac{1}{13}\int u^{12} (1-u^2) \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{1}{13}\int u^{12} -u^{14} \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{1}{13} \left[ \frac{u^{13}}{13} - \frac{u^{15}}{15} \right]+C \\\\ \amp = \frac{1}{13} \left[ \frac{\sin^{13}(13 x) }{13} - \frac{\sin^{15}(13 x)}{15} \right]+C \\\\ \end{aligned}

Thus the integral can be rewritten as \int 15\sin^{2}\mathopen{}\left(5x\right) \, dx = 15 \int \frac{ 1 - \cos(10 x)}{2} dx
And it could be calculated by continuing on:
Pulling out the constant turns the integral into two different, basic integrals. \frac{15}{2} \int \left( 1 - \cos(10 x) \right) \,dx = \frac{15}{2} \int dx - \frac{15}{2} \int \cos(10 x) \, dx
So this integrates to \frac{15 x}{2} - \frac{15 \sin(10 x)}{20} +C

hint.p: The integral involves \tan u and \sec u where the exponent of \tan u is odd and positive. So we rewrite in order to have a copy of \sec(-7 x) \tan(-7 x) and use a trigonometric identity to turn the remaining even powers of \tan(-7 x) into an expression of \sec^2(-7 x). Then use u-substitution with u= \sec(-7 x).

Thus the integral can be rewritten as \int 12\tan^{3}\mathopen{}\left(-7x\right)\sec^{3}\mathopen{}\left(-7x\right) \, dx = 12 \int \tan^2(-7 x) \sec^2(-7 x) \sec(-7 x) \tan(-7 x) \, dx = 12 \int \bigg( \sec^2(-7 x)-1 \bigg) \sec^2(-7 x) \sec(-7 x) \tan(-7 x) \, dx Now let u= \sec(-7 x).
Letting u= \sec(-7 x) means that du= -7 \sec(-7 x)\tan(-7 x) \, dx, and thus dx= \frac{du}{-7\sec(-7 x)\tan(-7 x)}.

So the integral turns into = 12 \int \bigg( u^2-1 \bigg) u^2 \sec(-7 x) \tan(-7 x) \frac{du}{-7\sec(-7 x)\tan(-7 x)} = \frac{12}{-7} \int \bigg( u^2-1 \bigg) u^2 \, du = \frac{12}{-7} \int \bigg( u^4-u^2 \bigg) \, du And each part can be integrated with power rule. Don't forget to plug back in what u equals!

solution.p: The integral involves \tan u and \sec u where the exponent of \tan u is odd and positive. So we rewrite in order to have a copy of \sec(-7 x) \tan(-7 x) and use a trigonometric identity to turn the remaining even powers of \tan(-7 x) into an expression of \sec^2(-7 x).

Then let u= \sec(-7 x), which means that du= -7 \sec(-7 x)\tan(-7 x) \, dx, and thus dx= \frac{du}{-7\sec(-7 x)\tan(-7 x)}. \begin{aligned} \int 12\tan^{3}\mathopen{}\left(-7x\right)\sec^{3}\mathopen{}\left(-7x\right) \, dx \amp = 12 \int \tan^2(-7 x) \sec^2(-7 x) \sec(-7 x) \tan(-7 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = 12 \int \bigg( \sec^2(-7 x)-1 \bigg) \sec^2(-7 x) \sec(-7 x) \tan(-7 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = 12 \int \bigg( u^2-1 \bigg) u^2 \sec(-7 x) \tan(-7 x) \frac{du}{-7\sec(-7 x)\tan(-7 x)} \\\\ \amp = \frac{12}{-7} \int \bigg( u^2-1 \bigg) u^2 \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{12}{-7} \int \bigg( u^4-u^2 \bigg) \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{12}{-7} \bigg[\frac{ u^5}{5}-\frac{u^3}{3}\bigg]+C \\\\ \amp = \frac{12}{-7} \bigg[\frac{ \sec^5(-7 x)}{5}-\frac{\sec^3(-7 x)}{3}\bigg]+C \end{aligned}
The correct trigonometric identity used is C.

solution.p: The integral involves \tan u and \sec u where the exponent of \sec u is even and positive. So we rewrite in order to have one copy of \sec^2(8 x) for the derivative, and use a trigonometric identity to turn the remaining even powers of \sec(8 x) into an expression of \tan^2(8 x).

Then let u= \tan(8 x), which means that du= 8 \sec^2(8 x) \, dx, and thus dx= \frac{du}{8\sec^2(8 x)}. \begin{aligned} \int 6\tan^{4}\mathopen{}\left(8x\right)\sec^{4}\mathopen{}\left(8x\right) \, dx \amp = 6 \int \tan^4(8 x) \sec^2(8 x) \sec^2(8 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = 6 \int \tan^4(8 x) \bigg( \tan^2(8 x)+1 \bigg) \sec^2(8 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = 6 \int u^4\bigg( u^2+1 \bigg) \sec^2(8 x) \frac{du}{8\sec^2(8 x)} \\\\ \amp = \frac{6}{8} \int u^4\bigg( u^2+1 \bigg) \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{6}{8} \int \bigg( u^6+u^4 \bigg) \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{6}{8} \bigg[\frac{ u^7}{7}+\frac{u^5}{5}\bigg]+C \\\\ \amp = \frac{6}{8} \bigg[\frac{ \tan^7(8 x)}{7}+\frac{\tan^5(8 x)}{5}\bigg]+C \end{aligned}
The correct trigonometric identity used is D.

Then let u= \csc(-10 x), which means that du= + 10 \csc(-10 x)\cot(-10 x) \, dx, and thus dx= \frac{du}{ + 10\csc(-10 x)\cot(-10 x)}. \begin{aligned} \int 10\cot^{3}\mathopen{}\left(-10x\right)\csc^{3}\mathopen{}\left(-10x\right) \, dx \amp = 10 \int \cot^2(-10 x) \csc^2(-10 x) \csc(-10 x) \cot(-10 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = 10 \int \bigg( \csc^2(-10 x)-1 \bigg) \csc^2(-10 x) \csc(-10 x) \cot(-10 x) \, dx \\\\ \amp = 10 \int \bigg( u^2-1 \bigg) u^2 \csc(-10 x) \cot(-10 x) \frac{du}{ + 10\csc(-10 x)\cot(-10 x)} \\\\ \amp = \frac{10}{ + 10} \int \bigg( u^2-1 \bigg) u^2 \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{10}{ + 10} \int \bigg( u^4-u^2 \bigg) \, du \\\\ \amp = \frac{10}{ + 10} \bigg[\frac{ u^5}{5}-\frac{u^3}{3}\bigg]+C \\\\ \amp = \frac{10}{ + 10} \bigg[\frac{ \csc^5(-10 x)}{5}-\frac{\csc^3(-10 x)}{3}\bigg]+C \end{aligned}

statement.p: Find the equation (in terms of x and y) of the tangent line to the curve r=2\sin5\theta at \theta=\pi/3.

static.solution: x and y as being parametrically equations with parameter \theta: x = r\cos(\theta) = 2 \sin(5\theta) \cos(\theta), \ \hbox{and}\ y = r\sin(\theta) = 2 \sin(5\theta) \sin(\theta). Then we know that the slope of the tangent line is {dy\over dx} = {dy/d\theta\over dx/d\theta}. Taking the derivatives, {dx\over d\theta} = 2(5\cos(5\theta)\cos(\theta) - \sin(5\theta)\sin(\theta)) and {dy\over d\theta} = 2(5\cos(5\theta)\sin(\theta) + \sin(5\theta)\cos(\theta)). Thus {dy\over dx} = {5\cos(5\theta)\sin(\theta) + \sin(5\theta)\cos(\theta) \over 5\cos(5\theta)\cos(\theta) - \sin(5\theta)\sin(\theta) }. We want this at \theta = \pi/3, so that we get {dy\over dx}\approx 0.866. Then, at \theta = \pi/3, x(\pi/3) = 2 \sin(5\cdot \pi/3)\cos(\pi/3) \approx -0.866, and y(\pi/3) = 2 \sin(5\cdot \pi/3)\sin(\pi/3) \approx -1.5, so that the tangent line is y \approx -1.5 + (0.866)(x + 0.866). (Note, however, that the correct answer may require more significant figures than are shown in this solution.)

static.solution:
r=4 - \cos \theta in r and \theta (cartesian, not polar, this time):
r_0=3 ,\quad r_1=4 \quad r_2=5
We see that as \theta varies from 0 to \pi, the radius r increases from 3 to 5,
so we get the upper half of the cardioid (the lower half is obtained as \theta varies from \pi to 2\pi and consequently r decreases from 5 to 3.
Since the cardioid is symmetric with respect to the x-axis we may compute the upper area and double the result.
Using \cos^{2}\theta =\frac{ \cos 2\theta +1}{2} we get A = 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi }{r}^{2} \,d\theta= \int_{0}^{\pi }{\left(4- \cos \theta \right)}^{2} \,d\theta= \int_{0}^{\pi}\left(16-8 \cos \theta +\cos^{2}\theta \right) \,d\theta= \int_{0}^{\pi}\left(16-8 \cos \theta +\frac{ \cos 2\theta +1}{2}\right)\,d\theta=\int_{0}^{\pi }\left(\frac{33}{2}-8 \cos \theta +\frac{1}{2} \cos 2\theta \right) \,d\theta = \frac{33}{2}\theta -8 \sin \theta +\frac{1}{4} \sin 2\theta \bigg|_{0}^{\pi }= \frac{33\pi }{2}

statement.p: Find the area of one leaf of the "four-petaled rose" r =5 \sin 2\theta shown in the following figure:
With r_0=5
Answer :

static.solution:
r=5 \sin 2\theta in cartesian coordinates:
With r_0=5
We see that as \theta varies from 0 to \frac{\pi }{4} the radius r is increasing from 0 to 5, and when \theta varies from \frac{\pi }{4} to \frac{\pi}{2}, r is decreasing back to zero.
Hence, the leaf in the first quadrant is traced as \theta varies from 0 to \frac{\pi }{2}. The area of the leaf (the four leaves have equal areas) is thus A=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{r}^{2} \,d\theta= \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} 25\sin^{2} 2\theta \,d\theta. Using the identity \sin^{2} 2\theta =\frac{1- \cos 4\theta }{2} we get A = 12.5\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{ \cos 4\theta }{2}\right) \,d\theta= 12.5\left(\frac{\theta }{2}-\frac{ \sin 4\theta}{8}\right)\bigg|_{0}^{\pi/2}= 12.5\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{ \sin 2\pi }{8}\right)-0\right)= \frac{12.5\pi }{4} The area of one leaf is A=\frac{12.5\pi }{4}\approx 9.817.

statement.p: Find the area lying outside r=4\sin\theta and inside r=2 + 2 \sin\theta.
Area =

static.solution:
r=4\sin\theta is a circle with radius 2 centered on (0,2), while r=2 + 2 \sin\theta is a cardioid that entirely encloses the circle. Therefore, to find the area, we subtract the area enclosed by the circle from that enclosed by the cardioid.
The cardioid, r=2 + 2 \sin\theta, is traced out as \theta goes from \theta=0 to \theta=2\pi. Thus, remembering that the area enclosed by a region lying within the polar equation r = f(\theta) is Area= \int_\alpha^\beta\,{1\over2}(f(\theta))^2\,d\theta, \hbox{Area of cardioid } = \int_0^{2\pi}{1\over2}(2 + 2 \sin\theta)^2\,d\theta. The circle is traced out as \theta goes from \theta=0 to \theta=\pi, so its area is \hbox{Area of circle }= \int_0^{\pi}{1\over2}(4\sin\theta)^2\,d\theta. Of course, because the circle has radius 2, we know this second integral will evaluate to 4 \pi.
We can find the area of the cardioid, \int_0^{2\pi}{1\over2}(2 + 2 \sin\theta)^2\,d\theta = {1\over2}\int_0^{2\pi} 4 (1 + 2\sin\theta + \sin^2\theta)\,d\theta, numerically by using a calculator, or by parts, or using a table of integrals, to find that the area of the cardioid is A = 6\pi.
Thus, the area enclosed by the cardioid that lies outside of the circle is given by A = 6\pi - 4\pi = 2\pi.
